295.title: I am who am (Exodus 3:14)
295.hook: the name God gives Moses at the burning bush
295.howItsDone: Catholics hear the burning bush read at Mass, and out of reverence the Church asks that the Hebrew divine name not be spoken aloud in the liturgy, where it is rendered as the Lord.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Magisterium: a teaching office that serves the word, not above it. Your line was servants of the word. Now, what does the word say about God himself? Day two hundred ninety-five.

A name tells you who someone is, or at least how to call them. Now imagine you're a shepherd on a mountain in the desert. A bush is on fire and doesn't burn up. A voice from it tells you to go back to Egypt, face Pharaoh, and lead a nation of slaves to freedom. And you ask the most reasonable question there is: who should I say sent me? What's your name? The answer Moses gets is hardly a name at all. Today: Aquinas.
screen: `A BUSH THAT DOESN'T BURN UP.` → `WHO SHOULD I SAY SENT ME?` → `HARDLY A NAME AT ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the answer. In the Douay-Rheims, God says to Moses: "I AM WHO AM." And then: tell the people of Israel, "HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you." In Hebrew it's three words, ehyeh asher ehyeh, built on the verb to be. Scholars still debate how to translate it: I am who I am, or I will be who I will be. Jews read and treasure this passage too, and traditionally don't pronounce the holy four-letter name God gives in the next verse. Second, a name that won't be pinned down. This is a name that refuses to be a handle. The Catechism says it's both revealed and mysterious: God tells Moses who he is, and at the same time stays beyond grasping. Third, being itself. Thomas Aquinas called HE WHO IS the most fitting name for God. For him, God doesn't just have existence, the way a tree or a star has it. God is existence. Everything else has its being on loan; God simply is. Remember young Merton on the train, nearly throwing out a philosophy book? This was the idea that stopped him. The Catechism calls God the fullness of being. Fourth, the Gospel echo. In John's Gospel, Jesus says: "Amen, amen I say to you, before Abraham was made, I AM." Christians hear in those words a claim to the name from the bush. Catholics take that to mean the God who simply is came close enough to be spoken to by name.
screen: `EHYEH ASHER EHYEH.` · `A NAME THAT ISN'T A HANDLE.` · `NOT A BEING, BUT BEING ITSELF.` · `BEFORE ABRAHAM WAS MADE, I AM.` · then, large: `I AM WHO AM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in being. Breathe in, and out. On the out-breath, say quietly, inside: I am. Not I am busy, or I am tired, or I am behind. Just: I am. Let the words go, and notice that you simply exist, right now, without doing anything to earn it. Catholics believe every moment of that existence is borrowed from God, who simply is. If you pray, you can rest there, held in being. The bell holds the time.
Aquinas, the theologian who called God's name at the bush, HE WHO IS, the most fitting name, because God simply is existence. Today's word.
Your line: being itself. Today, once, stop mid-rush and notice that you exist. No achievement needed. Just: I am. Day two hundred ninety-five.

296.title: God is charity (1 John 4:8)
296.hook: the Douay calls it charity: God's very being is love (CCC 221)
296.howItsDone: Catholics count charity, love of God and neighbor, as the greatest of the three theological virtues, and practice it through the corporal and spiritual works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I am who am, Aquinas: God's name at the burning bush, being itself. Your line was being itself. Did you stop once and notice you exist? Today, the Bible says what that being is like. Day two hundred ninety-six.

Say the word charity today and people picture a donation. A jar by the register, a fundraiser, a tax receipt in January. Good things, but a little distant. So it's a jolt to open an old Catholic Bible and find, in the first letter of John, the Douay-Rheims saying it plainly: God is charity. Not God gives to charity. God is charity. That old English word used to mean something much bigger and warmer than a donation. Today: agape.
screen: `A JAR BY THE REGISTER.` → `GOD IS CHARITY?` → `A BIGGER, WARMER WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. In the Douay-Rheims: "He that loveth not, knoweth not God: for God is charity." And a few lines later: "God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him." The Greek word is agape, the love that gives itself away for another's good. Saint Jerome's Latin Bible put it as Deus caritas est. And the Douay translators, working from that Latin, kept its word: charity. Second, the word itself. Caritas comes from carus, dear, precious. Charity once meant holding someone dear, loving them because they're precious. Over time, English shrank it down to donations. The old translation lets you hear the big meaning again. Third, the Catechism. Paragraph 221 says John's line reaches all the way down: love isn't just something God does, or feels now and then. God's very being is love. Tomorrow we'll see why Catholics say that love has a shape. For today, just this: in Catholic teaching, the God who told Moses I AM is, all the way through, love. Fourth, what it looks like. Paul describes charity in his first letter to the Corinthians: "Charity is patient, is kind: charity envieth not." It's often read at weddings. Paul's word there is agape too, so read beside John, it becomes a portrait of God. And it's why John can say the one who doesn't love doesn't know God. For Catholics, God is known less by argument than by love, given and received. In 2005, Pope Benedict XVI chose these three Latin words as the title of his first encyclical.
screen: `AGAPE, CARITAS, CHARITY.` · `CARUS — DEAR, PRECIOUS.` · `GOD'S VERY BEING IS LOVE.` · `CHARITY IS PATIENT, IS KIND.` · then, large: `GOD IS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one hidden kindness. Take one slow breath. Think of someone near you: at home, at work, down the street. What's one small loving thing you could do for them today that no one will notice? Refill something. Fix something. Pray for them. Write a kind word and leave it. Picture yourself doing it, quietly, with no credit. Jesus said to give so that your left hand doesn't know what your right hand is doing. If you pray, you can offer it ahead of time. The bell holds the time.
Agape, the Greek word behind 'God is charity': the love that gives itself away for another's good, which Catholics say is God's very being. Today's word.
Your line: god is love. Today, do your one loving act quietly, and tell no one. Let it be charity in the old, big sense. Day two hundred ninety-six.

297.title: The Trinity (CCC 253–256)
297.hook: one God in three persons, a communion of love
297.howItsDone: Catholics begin and end prayer with the sign of the cross in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, pray the Glory Be after each decade of the rosary, and keep Trinity Sunday the week after Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday: God is charity, agape, God's very being is love. Your line was god is love. Did you manage your hidden kindness? Today, a puzzle hiding in that line. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

Here's a question a kid might ask at the dinner table. If God is love, who did God love before there was anything? Before the world, before angels, before people. Love needs someone to love, doesn't it? You can't really be love all by yourself in an empty room. It sounds like a riddle. For Catholics, the answer is the most central mystery of the faith, the one they name every time they make the sign of the cross. Today: the Trinity.
screen: `WHO DID GOD LOVE BEFORE ANYTHING?` → `LOVE NEEDS SOMEONE TO LOVE.` → `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Catholics believe in one God in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Jesus sends his apostles out, in the Douay-Rheims: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Notice: in the name, singular. One name, three persons. Second, what it doesn't mean. The Catechism, in paragraphs 253 to 256, is careful. It's not three gods. It's not one God wearing three masks, either. Each person is fully God, and the three are really distinct from one another, distinct only in how they relate: the Father begets, the Son is begotten, the Spirit proceeds. Early councils, at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381, fought hard for that language, and nearly every Christian church still professes it in the Creed. Third, the answer to the riddle. If God is love, then from all eternity there is lover, beloved, and the love between them. Augustine put it almost that way sixteen centuries ago. God was never alone in an empty room. God is a communion, a life of self-giving love, before anything else existed. And creation, and each person, is invited into that love. Fourth, it's a mystery. The Catechism calls the Trinity the central mystery of Christian faith, something we couldn't have figured out, only received. There's a famous story that Saint Patrick used a three-leafed shamrock to explain it. It's a story people tell, not something in his own writings, and every picture falls short. The Church's honest answer is: this is who God is, and it's love all the way down.
screen: `ONE NAME, THREE PERSONS.` · `NOT THREE GODS, NOT THREE MASKS.` · `LOVER, BELOVED, AND LOVE.` · `THE CENTRAL MYSTERY.` · then, large: `LOVE IS A COMMUNION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray, or hear, the Glory Be, slowly. It's one of the oldest and shortest Catholic prayers. Breathe between each phrase. Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen. If you pray, say it once more on your own, slowly, then sit in the quiet after it. If you don't, just listen to its shape: three names, one glory, always. The bell holds the time.
The Trinity. One God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit: the central mystery of Catholic faith, a communion of love. Today's word.
Your line: love is a communion. Today, notice a moment of real togetherness, a shared laugh, a meal, a hand held, and let it remind you what Catholics say God is. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

298.title: Very good (Genesis 1:31)
298.hook: God made the world freely, out of goodness
298.howItsDone: Catholics profess God as creator of heaven and earth in the Creed at every Sunday Mass, bless animals on the feast of Saint Francis on October 4, and many now keep a Season of Creation each September.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Trinity: one God, a communion of love from all eternity. Your line was love is a communion. Where did you feel real togetherness? Today, that love spills over into a world. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

A Saturday, and a neighbor is building a garden bed nobody asked for. No one is paying her. She doesn't even need the tomatoes; the store sells them. She's doing it because something in her is full and wants to spill over. When the last board is in, she steps back, wipes her hands, looks, and says one word: good. The Bible's first chapter ends with God stepping back and looking, too. Today: creation.
screen: `A GARDEN BED NOBODY ASKED FOR.` → `FULL, AND SPILLING OVER.` → `STEPPING BACK: GOOD.`

segments.voice: First, the refrain. Genesis opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth." Then, day after day, as light and sea and plants and animals appear, the same line comes back: God saw that it was good. And at the end, after human beings are made: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." In Hebrew, tov me'od. Not just good. Very good. Second, why God made it. The Catechism says God didn't create because he needed anything. God created freely, out of wisdom and goodness, to share his own goodness. Remember yesterday: Catholics say God was never alone. So, in their telling, creation isn't God filling a gap. It's love spilling over. Third, out of nothing. Catholics believe God created not from some material already lying around, but from nothing at all. In that view, everything that exists, from galaxies to the dust on your windowsill, exists because God wants it to, right now. And here's a surprise: the Catechism says the six days are presented symbolically, a picture of God's work, not a stopwatch. Catholics are free to learn from science how the world developed. Fourth, what very good means for a Tuesday. The Catechism says each creature has its own particular goodness, reflecting something of God. Saint Francis of Assisi sang to Brother Sun and Sister Moon. Pope Francis took his 2015 letter on the environment, Laudato Si', from that song. For Catholics, a world God called very good is worth noticing, thanking, and caring for.
screen: `AND THEY WERE VERY GOOD.` · `NOT NEEDED, BUT SHARED.` · `OUT OF NOTHING, BY LOVE.` · `EACH CREATURE ITS OWN GOODNESS.` · then, large: `IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless one thing in nature. Look for something alive or natural near you: a plant on the sill, a tree through the window, the sky, a dog asleep, even your own breath. Look at it the way Genesis does: made on purpose, wanted into being. Let yourself say, inside: very good. If you pray, you can praise God for it, the way Francis did. If not, simply be glad it exists. The bell holds the time.
Creation. Everything God made freely, out of nothing, to share his goodness: and he called it very good. Today's word.
Your line: it was very good. Today, step outside for one minute, look at one living thing, and say it under your breath: very good. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

299.title: Why evil (CCC 309)
299.hook: no quick answer; the whole of the faith is the answer
299.howItsDone: Catholics bring suffering to prayer in many ways, including the psalms of lament, the Stations of the Cross, the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, and Masses offered for those who suffer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, creation: God made everything freely, and called it very good. Your line was it was very good. What living thing did you look at? Today, the question that line raises for everyone. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

A child in a hospital bed. A flood that takes a whole town. A friend who did everything right and got the diagnosis anyway. And the question shows up, sometimes shouted, sometimes whispered at two in the morning: if God is good, and God made all this very good, then why? People sometimes expect a religion to have a neat answer, one sentence, on a card. The Catechism of the Catholic Church doesn't give one. It says something more honest. Today: why evil.
screen: `A HOSPITAL BED. A FLOOD. A DIAGNOSIS.` → `IF GOD IS GOOD, WHY?` → `NO NEAT ANSWER ON A CARD.`

segments.voice: First, the honesty. Paragraph 309 asks the question straight: if God is almighty and good and cares for every creature, why does evil exist? And it says the question is as pressing as it is unavoidable, as painful as it is mysterious, and that no quick answer will do. For a book of teaching, that's a remarkable sentence. Second, the whole faith as answer. Instead of one line, the Catechism points to everything: the goodness of creation, the drama of human freedom and sin, God's patient love through the covenants, God becoming human in Jesus, the Spirit, the Church, the sacraments, and the promise of a life to come. It says there isn't a single part of the Christian message that isn't, in part, an answer to evil. Not an explanation. An answer, the way a friend who shows up is an answer. Third, good out of evil. The Catechism points to Joseph, sold as a slave by his own brothers. Years later, he tells them, in the Douay-Rheims: "You thought evil against me: but God turned it into good." Catholics believe God doesn't cause evil, but can bring good out of it, often in ways no one could see at the time. Fourth, God in it. For Catholics, the answer runs through the cross. Jesus doesn't explain suffering from a distance. He enters it. On the cross, Matthew says, he cries out the opening of a psalm of lament: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Even God's Son asked why. Catholics say you're allowed to ask it too, and that you won't ask it alone.
screen: `NO QUICK ANSWER WILL DO.` · `THE WHOLE FAITH IS THE ANSWER.` · `GOD TURNED IT INTO GOOD.` · `EVEN THE SON ASKED WHY.` · then, large: `NO QUICK ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit honestly with one hard question. Settle and breathe. Let one real why come up, about something that hurt you, or someone you love, or the world. Don't rush to answer it, and don't push it away. Just let it be there, in the open, like a stone in your hands. If you're angry, let that be honest too. Some psalms are angry. If you pray, you can bring the question to God as it is, unsolved. The bell holds the time.
Why evil. An old, hard question, which the Catechism answers not with a slogan but with the whole of the faith. Today's word.
Your line: no quick answer. Today, if someone near you is suffering, resist the urge to explain it. Show up instead. Be an answer, not a slogan. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

300.title: Angels (CCC 328–336)
300.hook: spiritual creatures, messengers, and a guardian beside each person
300.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Holy Guardian Angels on October 2 and of the archangels Michael, Gabriel and Raphael on September 29, and many families teach children the guardian angel prayer at bedtime.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why evil: the hard question, and the Catechism's honest answer that no quick answer will do. Your line was no quick answer. Did you show up for someone? Today, day three hundred, and some company for the road. Day three hundred.

Angels are everywhere in our culture. Chubby babies with harps on greeting cards. Women in white robes on top of Christmas trees. People say someone who died has become an angel now. A sweet kid gets called an angel. Almost none of that is what the Catholic Church actually teaches about angels. What it does teach is stranger, and in a way more comforting: that you have never, for one moment of your life, been completely alone. Today: angels.
screen: `HARPS, ROBES, CHRISTMAS TREES.` → `NOT WHAT THE CHURCH TEACHES.` → `NEVER COMPLETELY ALONE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Angel comes from the Greek angelos, messenger. Augustine made a sharp point about it, and the Catechism repeats it: angel is the name of their job, not their nature. What they are is spirit. What they do is carry God's messages. Think of Gabriel at Nazareth, telling Mary she would bear a son. Second, what they are. The Catechism, from paragraph 328, says the existence of angels is a truth of faith. They are purely spiritual creatures, with intelligence and will, personal and immortal. And they're created. They are not God, and, despite the greeting cards, they're not people who died. When someone dies, Catholics pray they're with God, and the Church teaches they don't become angels. Third, the guardian. Jesus says, in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "See that you despise not one of these little ones: for I say to you, that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven." And a psalm promises: "For he hath given his angels charge over thee; to keep thee in all thy ways." The Catechism says that from infancy to death, human life is surrounded by the angels' watchful care, and quotes Saint Basil: beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd. Fourth, never alone. Catholics keep the feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2, and there's a short traditional prayer to the guardian angel, often taught to children. It's a small, steady comfort: on the dark nights, in the hospital hallway, on the drive home, Catholics believe someone God sent is keeping watch.
screen: `ANGELOS — MESSENGER.` · `SPIRITS, NOT PEOPLE WHO DIED.` · `AN ANGEL BESIDE EACH BELIEVER.` · `THE FEAST OF OCTOBER 2.` · then, large: `TO KEEP THEE IN ALL THY WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the guardian angel prayer. It's short enough for a child to learn by heart. Angel of God, my guardian dear, to whom God's love commits me here, ever this day be at my side, to light and guard, to rule and guide. Amen. If you pray, say it once, slowly, on your own. If you don't, sit with the idea for a minute: that someone might be keeping watch beside you, right now. Notice how that feels. The bell holds the time.
Angel. From the Greek for messenger: a spiritual creature made by God, and in Catholic belief, a guardian beside each person. Today's word.
Your line: never alone. Three hundred days on the path. Today, in one lonely moment, remember the Church's promise: someone is keeping watch. Day three hundred.

301.title: In his image (CCC 356–357)
301.hook: every human being is someone, not something
301.howItsDone: Catholics learn in catechism that every person is made in the image of God, and the Church's social teaching on the poor, the unborn, the sick, migrants and prisoners is built on that dignity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, angels: spiritual messengers, and, the Church says, a guardian beside each person. Your line was never alone. Did you catch a moment when you felt accompanied? Today, the creature those guardians are sent to watch over. Day three hundred one.

Listen to how we talk about people on an ordinary day. The delivery. The new hire. The guy in 4B. My ride is two minutes away. The customer on line three. None of it is cruel. It's just fast. A person becomes the job they're doing for us, and we move on. The first chapter of the Bible says the opposite. It puts an invisible mark on every one of those people: this one was made on purpose, to the image of God. The Catechism turns it into a short phrase: a person is someone, not something.
screen: `THE DELIVERY. THE NEW HIRE. THE GUY IN 4B.`
`A MARK YOU CAN'T SEE.` → `SOMEONE, NOT SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Start with the text. On the sixth day, in the Douay-Rheims, God says: "Let us make man to our image and likeness." And then: "And God created man to his own image: to the image of God he created him. Male and female he created them." In Latin, image of God is imago Dei, and that's today's word. Second, what an image was. In the ancient world, some scholars point out, kings set up statues of themselves in the lands they ruled, a way of saying: I'm present here, this belongs to me. Genesis takes that royal idea and hands it to everyone. Not only the king. The farmer, the servant, the child. Every human being is God's image set down in the world. Third, what the Catechism does with it. It teaches that the human person is the only creature on earth God willed for its own sake, and that each of us is able to know ourselves, to give ourselves freely, and to enter into friendship with God. That's why the Church says a person has dignity: not a thing to be used, but someone. Early Christian writers added a detail. Some, like Irenaeus, told image and likeness apart. The image, they said, is never lost. The likeness, a life that actually resembles God, can be damaged and restored. Fourth, the hard part. The image is in everyone or it means nothing. The person you admire, yes. And the person who cut you off in traffic, the prisoner, the stranger whose language you don't speak, the baby, the dying. Catholics ground their social teaching right here: in this one verse about who we are.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at someone as God's image. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one face you saw today, maybe someone you barely noticed: the cashier, a driver, a coworker. Hold their face for a moment. Say to yourself, quietly: someone, not something. Then, if you can, bring to mind a face that's harder, someone who annoys you. Hold that face too. You don't have to feel warm. Just let them be a person for a minute. If you pray, you can offer each face to God. The bell holds the time.
